# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–27 (Complete – Updated 195)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn in continental Europe, seventh year after Waterloo**. John Sedley deceased (died peacefully in sleep; buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife). Mr. Osborne deceased (died four days after stroke; found at foot of dressing-table). Major Dobbin appointed executor of Osborne's will. Rawdon governs Coventry Island. Georgy established as heir. **Continental tour progressing**: Amelia, Georgy, Jos, and Major Dobbin on steamship and carriage tour; landed Rotterdam, traveled to Cologne, now established in Pumpernickel (a small German principality) for autumn/winter season.
- **Major locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn, Haymarket Theatre, Gillespie Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Piccadilly; Madras; St. Helena; Cape; Southampton; Staveton; Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John); Bengal; Salford; Regent's Park; Richmond (Star and Garter); Gulton; Harrowgate; Hill farms; Roehampton; Hampton Court; Calcutta; Jamaica; Rotterdam; Cologne; Free City of Judenstadt; Rhine region; Rhineland; **Pumpernickel** (small German principality with Court, theatre, Duke's schloss, Prime Minister's lodgings, Aurelius Platz, Zwieback's Conditorey, Saint Michael's Fountain, Artillery Place, Stadthaus, Town Hall, Redoute, gardens with Trophonius' cave, nymphbath, Niagara cataract); Mirecombe; Dunholt; Dunwick; Quenwick; Humbourg-Schlippenschloppen; Ems; Aix-la-Chapelle; Baden-Baden; Salwick; Elephant (lodging-house); Boulogne (French coast refuge); Albion/England; Salmere; Dieppe; Waterloo; Laeken; Brussels; Paris; Wildbad; Strasburg.

## John Sedley's Final Illness and Death (Chapter 26)
Amelia nursed father devotedly during final illness. Old Sedley forgave past grievances, confessing unkindness to Amelia. Died peacefully in sleep. Buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife. Major Dobbin, Jos, and Georgy followed remains to grave.

## Mr. Osborne's Stroke and Death (Chapter 26)
Osborne's mind visibly changing in final months. Asked Georgy about Jos; invited Jos and Dobbin to dinner where every family plate was exhibited. Osborne asked Dobbin repeatedly about Mrs. George Osborne. Dobbin spoke eloquently of Amelia's sufferings, passionate attachment to husband's memory, tender duty to parents, sacrifice of boy. Osborne replied: "By God, you are a good feller, sir." Reconciliation meeting never took place. Old Sedley's lingering illness intervened. Osborne found in dressing-room at foot of dressing-table in fit. Pocket of dressing-gown contained letter from George written from Waterloo and key to box of son's papers; seals broken—likely read night before seizure. Died in four days without speaking again.

**Will Terms**: Half property left to George Osborne (minor); remainder between two sisters. Mr. Bullock to continue commercial house affairs. **Annuity**: Five hundred pounds, chargeable on George's property, left to Amelia, "the widow of my beloved son, George Osborne," who was to resume guardianship of boy. Major William Dobbin appointed executor, named "my beloved son's friend." Will bequeathed sum "sufficient to purchase his commission as a Lieutenant-Colonel, or to be disposed of in any way he may think fit." Will showed "the hatred which he had so long cherished had gone out of his heart."

## Amelia's Transformation and New Life (Chapter 26)
Upon learning of William's bounty supporting her in poverty, Amelia "sank on her knees, and prayed for blessings on that constant and kind heart." Visited deserted Gaunt House in deep sables. At George's upper room window, looked out over Russell Square toward her birthplace. Thought of "man who had been her constant protector, her good genius, her sole benefactor, her tender and generous friend." Took temporary house at Richmond. During continental tour, discovered Dobbin's true gentlemanly character—generous aims, constant truth, elevated degree, lack of meanness making him simple, honest face, warm and humble heart. "Emmy, in this happy time, found that hers underwent a very great change in respect of the merits of the Major."

## Continental Tour (Chapter 26)
Party landed Rotterdam, traveled by steamer to Cologne. Jos announced arrival in Cologne newspapers as "Herr Graf Lord von Sedley nebst Begleitung aus London." Had court dress; insisted Dobbin bring regimental paraphernalia; announced intention to be presented at foreign courts. Left own card and Major's on "Our Minister" wherever party stopped. Kept journal noting defects or excellences of inns and wines. Observed Earl of Bareacres and family on ship; both "looked rather younger" than remembered from Brussels in '15, with Lady's dark hair now "a beautiful golden auburn" and Lord's red whiskers now "of a rich black with purple and green reflections." Amelia very happy and pleased. Dobbin carried her stool and sketch-book, admired her drawings. She sat upon steamers' decks and drew crags and castles, or mounted upon donkeys to ascend ancient robber-towers, attended by Georgy and Dobbin. She laughed at Major's droll figure on donkey-back. "Perhaps it was the happiest time of both their lives...this couple were very decently contented, and enjoyed as pleasant a summer tour as any pair that left England that year."

## Pumpernickel Arrival and Society (Chapter 26–27)
**Theatre and British Recognition**: Party attended theatre. Upon "burst of that beloved and well-known music," every Englishman in house proclaimed membership in British nation—"Sir John and Lady Bullminster (who had taken a house at Pumpernickel for the education of their nine children), the fat gentleman with the mustachios, the long Major in white duck trousers, and the lady with the little boy." Tapeworm, Charge d'Affaires (nephew and heir of old Marshal Tiptoff, now deceased), rose in his box and bowed.

**Tapeworm's Attentions**: Near end of performance, Tapeworm approached Jos with "fascinating smile" and invitation to stay in Pumpernickel. Accepted Jos's invitation to lodge at his quarters. Put dexterous questions to Jos about India and dancing-girls; asked Amelia about "that beautiful boy" (Georgy); complimented her upon "prodigious sensation which she had made in the house"; tried to fascinate Dobbin talking of late war and Pumpernickel contingent exploits. Doctor von Glauber speedily convinced Jos that Pumpernickel mineral springs and Doctor's particular treatment would "infallibly restore the Bengalee to youth and slimness." Jos's mind made up; committed to spend autumn in Pumpernickel. Next day, Tapeworm presented Jos and Major to Victor Aurelius XVII, conducted by Count de Schlusselback, Marshal of the Court. Straightway invited to dinner at Court. Upon announcement of intention to stay, "politest ladies of the whole town instantly called upon Mrs. Osborne"; as not one was under rank of Baroness, "Jos's delight was beyond expression." **Advancement**: Tapeworm's transparent (representing young Couple advancing and Discord flying away, with ludicrous likeness to French Ambassador) beat French picture hollow; likely got Tapeworm the advancement and the Cross of the Bath which he subsequently attained.

**Emmy at Court and Evening Dress**: Emmy presented to august family. On certain days mourning not admitted at Court, so she appeared in pink crape dress with diamond ornament in corsage presented by her brother. "She looked so pretty in this costume that the Duke and Court (putting out of the question the Major, who had scarcely ever seen her before in an evening dress, and vowed that she did not look five-and-twenty) all admired her excessively."

**Pumpernickel Government and Society**: Constitution moderate despotism tempered by Chamber that might or might not be elected. Prime Minister lodged in second floor; Foreign Secretary occupied comfortable lodgings over Zwieback's Conditorey. Army consisted of magnificent band that also did duty on stage. Noble society divided into factions: Strumpff faction (supported by Tapeworm, English) and Lederlung party (supported by French Charge d'Affaires M. de Macabau). Politics ran very high; parties very bitter. Strumpff was greater singer, stout, not in first youth and beauty; Lederlung pretty creature with sweet voice. Two women were "two flags of the French and the English party at Pumpernickel." Theatre known and famous in that quarter of Germany. Court conducted with comfort and splendour. Gardens arranged to emulate those of Versailles; allegorical waterworks include Trophonius' cave with leaden Tritons spouting water and playing groans from lead conchs, nymphbath, Niagara cataract.

**Emmy's Social Activities (Chapter 27)**: Before winter far advanced, Emmy took night and received company with great propriety and modesty. Had French master who complimented her upon purity of accent and facility of learning. Madam Strumpff came to give her lessons in singing, performed so well with such true voice that Major's windows opposite (lodgings under Prime Minister) were always open to hear lesson. German ladies, very sentimental and simple, fell in love with her and called her du at once. Major made himself George's tutor, read Caesar and mathematics with him; they had German master and rode out of evenings by side of Emmy's carriage. Emmy too timid, made dreadful outcry at slightest disturbance on horse-back. Drove about with one of dear German friends, Jos asleep on back-seat of barouche.

## Georgy Osborne (Chapter 26–27)
Now eleven years old; boy's "quick brain" revealed grandfather "a dullard." Day boy at Reverend Lawrence Veal's School (Hart Street, Bloomsbury). Marked aristos in Greek, optimus in Latin, très bien in French. On continental tour: walked ahead during excursions, climbing towers and trees, while Amelia and Dobbin walked soberly below. Made "prodigious advance in the knowledge of High Dutch" conversing with Herr Kirsch on carriage box. Now heir to half Osborne's substantial property. Will restored him to mother's guardianship. Boy remained active, imperious, good-natured.

**At Pumpernickel Wedding Festivities (Chapter 27)**: Got sausage wrenching it off pole at games during wedding festivities of Hereditary Prince of Pumpernickel with Princess Amelia of Humbourg-Schlippenschloppen; gave sausage to peasant standing at foot of mast. **At Gambling**: With relations away at Court festival, Georgy came to Stadthaus Ball with uncle's courier Kirsch. Hankered round roulette and trente-et-quarante tables (only allowed for week of festivities). Major Dobbin instantly went up to Georgy and pulled him briskly back from place of temptation, showing him eloquently why he shouldn't be there, would have enforced precepts by example of Georgy's own father, had he liked to say anything reflecting on other's memory. Major then housed him and went to bed, noting when his light in little room outside Amelia's presently disappeared.

## Jos's Activities at Pumpernickel (Chapter 27)
**Romantic Interest**: Jos becoming very sweet upon Grafinn Fanny de Butterbrod, very gentle tender-hearted and unassuming young creature, a Canoness and Countess in her own right but with scarcely ten pounds per year to her fortune. Fanny declared that to be Amelia's sister was greatest delight Heaven could bestow. Jos might have put Countess's shield and coronet by side of own arms on carriage and forks.

**At Gambling**: At Stadthaus, Jos remained behind over play-table; no gambler but not averse to little excitement of sport now and then, had some Napoleons chinking in embroidered pockets of court waistcoat. Put down one over fair shoulder of little gambler before him, and they won. Woman made little movement to make room for him. Jos sat down. Woman said archly: "Come and give me good luck," in foreign accent. She continued in pretty French accent, revealing knowledge of Georgy as image of his father, noting Jos's changes, lamenting her own unhappiness. Mentioned seeing "dear Amelia" that day, how pretty and happy she looked. Revealed herself as **Rebecca (Madame de Raudon)**, formerly involved with Rawdon Crawley.

## Rebecca's Degradation and Wanderings (Chapter 27)
**Moral Decline**: "This abattement and degradation did not take place all at once; it was brought about by degrees, after her calamity, and after many struggles to keep up--as a man who goes overboard hangs on to a spar whilst any hope is left, and then flings it away and goes down, when he finds that struggling is in vain." **Period of despair**: "There was period in Mrs. Becky's life when she was seized, not by remorse, but by kind of despair, and absolutely neglected her person and did not even care for her reputation."

**After Curzon Street Catastrophe and Duel**: Lingered in London while Rawdon prepared for departure to Coventry Island. Made more than one attempt to see Sir Pitt Crawley but never succeeded; Lady Jane interposed. Rebecca did not try to see or write to Pitt at his own house after initial attempts; correspondence regarding conjugal differences carried on by lawyers only.

**Wenham's Poisoning of Pitt's Mind**: Short time after Lord Steyne's accident, Wenham gave Baronet biography of Mrs. Becky astonishing member for Queen's Crawley. Becky left with "sad sad reputation in the esteem of a country gentleman and relative who had been once rather partial to her."

**Financial Settlement**: Revenues of Governor of Coventry Island not large. Part set aside by Rawdon for payment of outstanding debts and liabilities. Rawdon proposed to pay Becky only three hundred pounds a year on undertaking she would never trouble him. Otherwise, scandal, separation, Doctors' Commons would ensue.

**Boulogne Refuge**: First flight not very far. Perched upon French coast at Boulogne, refuge of so much exiled English innocence. Lived in rather genteel, widowed manner with femme de chambre and couple of rooms at hotel. Dined at table d'hote where people thought her very pleasant. Entertained neighbours by stories of brother Sir Pitt and great London acquaintance. Passed with many for person of importance. Gave little tea-parties in private room and shared in innocent amusements of place. Mrs. Burjoice voted her charming until little rogue Burjoice began paying too much attention. Becky always affable, easy, good-natured—especially with men. Found out by behaviour of acquaintances opinion of "society" regarding her conduct. Confronted by Lady Partlet and daughters walking modestly on pier; Lady Partlet marshalled all daughters round her with sweep of parasol and retreated, darting savage glances. Lady Slingstone arrived by packet, gave glance of scorn such as would have shrivelled up most women. Becky only laughed; but "I don't think she liked it. She felt she was alone, quite alone, and the far-off shining cliffs of England were impassable to her." Behaviour of men underwent change. Grinstone showed his teeth and laughed in her face with familiarity not pleasant. Little Bob Suckling, who was cap in hand to her three months before, nodded to her over his shoulder without moving his hat. Tom Raikes tried to walk into her sitting-room at inn with cigar in mouth. Becky felt very lonely. She thought about Rawdon "with great sadness and perhaps longing--about his honest, stupid, constant kindness and fidelity; his never-ceasing obedience; his good humour; his bravery and courage." Insults of women worse than male insults. Mrs. Crackenbury and Mrs. Washington White patronized her with sympathy and condescension until drove her almost wild with rage.

**Received Notice to Quit**: After paying her weekly bills and making herself agreeable to everybody in house, Becky received notice to quit from landlord, who had been told she was quite an unfit person to have at his hotel, where English ladies would not sit down with her. Forced to fly into lodgings of which the dulness and solitude were most wearisome to her.

**Attempted Respectability**: Still she held up, in spite of these rebuffs, and tried to make a character for herself and conquer scandal. She went to church very regularly and sang louder than anybody there. She took up cause of widows of shipwrecked fishermen, and gave work and drawings for Quashyboo Mission; she subscribed to Assembly and WOULDN'T waltz. "She did everything that was respectable, and that is why we dwell upon this part of her career with more fondness than upon subsequent parts of her history, which are not so pleasant." She saw people avoiding her, and still laboriously smiled upon them; you never could suppose from her countenance what pangs of humiliation she might be enduring inwardly.

**Mrs. Hook Eagles and Dieppe**: Mrs. Hook Eagles took her up at Dieppe—a woman without a blemish in her character and a house in Portman Square. They made each other's acquaintance first at sea, swimming together, and subsequently at table d'hote. Mrs. Eagles pronounced that Mrs. Crawley was an angel, her husband a ruffian, Lord Steyne an unprincipled wretch, and the whole case against Mrs. Crawley an infamous and wicked conspiracy of Wenham. Becky was very respectable and orderly at first, but the life of humdrum virtue grew utterly tedious to her before long. Young Mr. Eagles came from Cambridge, and his mother, seeing the impression which her little friend made upon him, straightway gave Becky warning.

**Brussels Journey and Recollections**: She grinned as she looked up at the little entresol which she had occupied at Brussels, and thought of Bareacres family. She went to Waterloo and to Laeken, where George Osborne's monument much struck her. She made a little sketch of it. "That poor Cupid!" she said; "how dreadfully he was in love with me, and what a fool he was! I wonder whether little Emmy is alive. It was a good little creature; and that fat brother of hers. I have his funny fat picture still among my papers. They were kind simple people."

**Brussels Gambling and Degradation**: At Brussels Becky arrived, recommended by Madame de Saint Amour to Madame la Comtesse de Borodino, widow of Napoleon's General, the famous Count de Borodino, left with no resource but a table d'hote and an ecarte table. Second-rate dandies and roues, widow-ladies who always have a lawsuit, and very simple English folks put down their money or ate their meals at Madame de Borodino's tables. Here, as at Paris, Becky was a boarding-house queen, ruled in select pensions. She never refused champagne, bouquets, drives into the country, or private boxes; but she preferred ecarte at night and played audaciously. First she played only for a little, then for five-franc pieces, then for Napoleons, then for notes: then she would not be able to pay her month's pension: then she borrowed from young gentlemen: then she got into cash again and bullied Madame de Borodino, whom she had coaxed and wheedled before: then she was playing for ten sous at a time, in dire state of poverty: then her quarter's allowance would come in, and she would pay off Madame de Borodino's score and would once more take the cards against Monsieur de Rossignol, or the Chevalier de Raff.

**Departure from Brussels**: When Becky left Brussels, the sad truth is that she owed three months' pension to Madame de Borodino, of which fact, and of the gambling, and of the drinking, and of the going down on her knees to Reverend Mr. Muff, Ministre Anglican, and borrowing money of him, and of her coaxing and flirting with Milor Noodle, son of Sir Noodle, pupil of Rev. Mr. Muff, whom she used to take into her private room, and of whom she won large sums at ecarte--of which fact, Countess de Borodino informs every English person who stops at her establishment, and announces that Madame Rawdon was no better than a vipere.

**Wanderings and Bohemian Life**: "So our little wanderer went about setting up her tent in various cities of Europe, as restless as Ulysses or Bampfylde Moore Carew. Her taste for disrespectability grew more and more remarkable. She became a perfect Bohemian ere long, herding with people whom it would make your hair stand on end to meet."

**Musical Performances and Reputation**: **RUMOR/CLAIM (per Mr. Eaves and others)**: When Mrs. Crawley was particularly down on her luck, she gave concerts and lessons in music here and there. There was a Madame de Raudon, who certainly had a matinee musicale at Wildbad, accompanied by Herr Spoff, premier pianist to Hospodar of Wallachia. Mr. Eaves, who knew everybody and had travelled everywhere, always used to declare that he was at Strasburg in 1830, when a certain Madame Rebecque made her appearance in the opera of the Dame Blanche, giving occasion to a furious row in the theatre. She was hissed off the stage by audience, partly from her own incompetency, but chiefly from ill-advised sympathy of some persons in the parquet (where officers of the garrison had their admissions); and Eaves was certain that unfortunate debutante in question was no other than Mrs. Rawdon Crawley.

## Other Reconciliations (Chapter 26)
Mrs. Frederick Bullock, "although despoiled by that little monster of one-half of the sum which she expected from her father, nevertheless showed her charitableness of spirit by being reconciled to the mother and the boy." One day chariot with golden bullocks emblazoned on panels drove to Amelia's house. Bullock family made irruption into garden where Amelia was reading, Jos in arbour dipping strawberries into wine, Major in Indian jacket giving back to Georgy for jumping over him. Miss Swartz and husband came thundering over from Hampton Court with flaming yellow liveries, "as impetuously fond of Amelia as ever."

## Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 23–24, 27)
Governor of Coventry Island, three thousand per year. Complete moral transformation: maintains honor, fulfills obligations, provides for son's education, compensates wronged. Separated from Rebecca permanently after duel with Steyne. Financial settlement with Rebecca: pays her three hundred pounds per year on undertaking she would never trouble him.
